newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Serbs must stay, vote - Western envoys.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Serbs must stay, vote - Western envoys.

text.p: Western diplomats on Friday urged Croatian Serbs from the Eastern Slavonia enclave to accept that the area's return to Zagreb rule was inevitable.
The diplomats also advised them to stay and vote in the first post-war elections next month.

Britain's ambassador to Croatia, Gavin Hewitt, and 12 other ambassadors visited Eastern Slavonia on Thursday for talks with local Serb leaders and officials of the 5,000-strong U.N. mission (UNTAES), which monitors the enclave until July 15.

"The Serb leaders have to persuade the people (in the enclave) to stay, take Croatian documents and to vote, excercising their civic and political rights as citizens of Croatia," Hewitt told a news conference in Zagreb.

"They must take full advantage of what is on offer," the diplomat added, referring to a human and minority rights package Zagreb has offered to the Serbs in the "Letter of reintegration of Eastern Slavonia".

The United Nations Security Council endorsed the letter and gave Zagreb the green light to go ahead with voting for local administrative bodies. The poll is scheduled for March 16, simultaneously with local election elsewhere in Croatia.

Eastern Slavonia broke away from Croatia in 1991, opposing its drive for independence from federal Yugoslavia. Croatia wants to take full control of the enclave after the UNTAES mandate expiry on July 15 and allow the return of all non-Serb refugees expelled from there since 1991.

The Serbs have dismissed Croatia's latest offer, demanding further concessions, primarily that the area should remain a single administrative unit with more autonomy and not be divided in two counties, as Zagreb would have it.
The Serb leadership, Hewitt said, was confusing its people by "prevaricating on the issue (of reintegration) for years". "They haven't got the leadership they deserve," he added.
"We told them procrastination is no way forward... There is no room, no time for further delay," the diplomat added.
"We also made clear the international community was interested in their future in terms of their human and civic rights but also that what is offered is a sound basis for that future."
The 13 ambassadors had emphasized it was Croatia's responsibility to stick to its promises, especially to make sure "every elligible citizen (in the enclave) gets his papers".
"If there are any problems (with the papers) Croatian authorities will be responsible," Hewit said.

The Croatian Foreign Ministry said on Thursday it had issued citizenship papers necessary for voters to 57,000 people or two thirds of the Eastern Slavonia population. The U.N. has put the number of current residents higher, at roughly 120,000.
Many of them are Serb refugees from other rebel enclaves Zagreb retook militarily in 1995.
Hewitt admitted some Serbs would probably leave the area ahead of the election. "It's inevitable consequence of the uncertainty their leadership has created by wrong political actions".

"Any person leaving Croatia at this time must be making the wrong economic decision... The area needs huge financial resources for economic restructuring... It deserves it, but as part of Croatia and not a particular separate area," he said.
